To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the parameters of an infinite variance stable limit distribution can be expressed in terms of the tail behavior of the underlying stationary process.

the partial sums of a stationary sequence of random variables with infinite variance converge in distribution to a stable distribution with index $\alpha\in(1,2)$ if and only if the partial sums of the absolute values of these random variables are regularly varying with index $\alpha$, and the tail of the stationary sequence is regularly varying with index $1/\alpha$ and a certain tail dependence coefficient.

the partial sums of a stationary process, with infinite variance, converges to a stable distribution if the partial sums of the squares of the process converge to a stable distribution, and the tail of the distribution of the squares is heavier than the tail of the original process.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the asymptotic behavior of sums of random variables which are not identically distributed, but are dependent and possess heavy tails.

the following problem: Let $X_1, X_2,...$ be a strictly stationary sequence of random variables with mean zero and let $Y_n = \sum_{i=1}^n a_iX_i$ where $a_1, a_2,...$ is a sequence of positive real numbers.

the following question: under which conditions on a stationary sequence of random variables, does the sum of a fixed number of random variables from this sequence converge in distribution to a stable distribution?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results of the present paper provide a general framework to derive stable convergence of sums of dependent random variables.
the partial sum of the absolute values of the innovations in a stationary process is asymptotically stable with index $\alpha=1/2$ if and only if the process has finite variance.

the partial sums of the squares of the GARCH( 1,1) process converge in distribution, as the sample size goes to infinity, to an infinite variance normal distribution, while the partial sums of a stochastic volatility model, with a finite second moment, converge to a stable distribution.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the stable limit of partial sums for these processes can be characterized by their tail characteristics.
the partial sums of a large class of time series models converge in distribution to infinite variance stable laws.
the tail behavior of a stationary process is a good predictor for the tail behavior of its partial sums.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in many cases, the limiting stable parameters can be computed in terms of the first two moments of the underlying stationary process.
the tail characteristics of a stationary sequence are sufficient to determine the tail behavior of the partial sums of the sequence.

in the case of a GARCH(1, 1) model with infinite second moment and infinite fourth moment, the partial sums of the squared innovations converge in distribution to a stable distribution with exponent between two and three.
